summary: This specification extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 so a mobile router can obtain IP prefixes for its attached mobile networks using DHCPv6 prefix delegation. The network provides mobility support for those prefixes, as it does for other addresses.

eli5.summary: A moving train needs a block of addresses for all the devices on board. This explains how the network hands the train a block and keeps it working as the train moves.

subtitle: How a Proxy Mobile IPv6 network hands a mobile router whole address prefixes and keeps them working as the router moves.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 gave mobility support to individual hosts, but there was no mobility support for whole networks attached to a mobile router.
tldr.mechanism: A new Delegated Mobile Network Prefix option is carried in Proxy Binding Update and Acknowledgement messages between the mobile access gateway and the local mobility anchor, so delegated prefixes (obtained through DHCPv6 prefix delegation or static configuration) are anchored and tunneled like a home address.
tldr.outcome: The delegated prefixes keep working when the mobile router changes its point of attachment, and the local fixed nodes behind it do not notice the move.

today: RFC 7148 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2014. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: Networks That Move
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6, RFC 5213) gives an IP host mobility support without the host taking part in any mobility signaling. A mobile access gateway (MAG) does the work on the host's behalf, and a local mobility anchor (LMA) is the home agent and topological anchor point.

That support is per host. The RFC states that there is currently no mobility support for the mobile networks attached to a mobile router (MR) in a PMIPv6 domain. This document adds it. The LMA does not track the individual nodes in the mobile network. It tracks a single mobile router session and associates the delegated prefixes with that session.

The signaling can also carry IPv4 subnets, but delegating IPv4 subnets to the mobile router is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The network already knew how to keep one phone connected while it moves. It did not know how to do that for a whole bus full of phones behind one router. This fixes that.

sections.title: Key Terms and Assumptions
sections.content:
The mobile router is a mobile node with extra routing capability. Its egress interface attaches to the MAG, and its ingress interfaces attach to the mobile network. A mobile network is an IP network attached to the mobile router, and local fixed nodes (LFNs) are the IP nodes inside it. They all move together as a single cluster.

A Delegated Mobile Network Prefix (DMNP) is an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix delegated to the mobile router and hosted in the mobile network. It is topologically anchored on the LMA.

The document assumes the mobile router is an IPv4 and/or IPv6 router with no mobility management of its own. It assumes DHCPv6 prefix delegation (RFC 3633) together with the Prefix Exclude Option (RFC 6603) as the default way to assign prefixes, and that the mobile router makes its DHCPv6 requests from its egress interface.
sections.eli5: The router is the bus driver's radio, the devices are the passengers, and the prefix is the block of seat numbers handed out. The whole bus travels as one group.

sections.title: Three Deployment Models
sections.content:
The RFC describes three ways to wire this together. In each, the mobile router first attaches and the usual PMIPv6 registration sets up a bidirectional tunnel between MAG and LMA.

  • Delegating router on the MAG. The MR acts as a DHCPv6 requesting router and sends a Solicit. The MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update carrying a DMNP option with an ALL_ZERO value, which asks the LMA to allocate prefixes. The prefixes come back in the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement and are then handed out in a DHCPv6 Reply. The RFC calls this the simplest option, since there is a single protocol interface between MAG and LMA.
  • Delegating router on the LMA. The MAG runs a DHCPv6 relay agent and forwards the DHCPv6 exchange to the LMA. The MAG then reports the delegated prefixes in a Proxy Binding Update so the LMA routes traffic for them through the tunnel. The relay SHOULD include the relay agent remote-id option so MR identities used over DHCPv6 and PMIPv6 can be correlated, and it has to queue the Reply while PMIPv6 signaling finishes.
  • Static configuration. The prefixes sit in the mobile node's policy profile. The MAG reads them and registers them with the LMA in the DMNP option. The mobile router sends no trigger, and as long as a mobility session exists for its home address, the LMA supports the prefixes.

A delegating router located elsewhere in the home network is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Who hands out the block of addresses can be the first stop, the home base, or a pre-written list. In every case the home base ends up knowing where to send mail for that block.

sections.title: The Delegated Mobile Network Prefix Option
sections.content:
The new mobility header option is used in Proxy Binding Update and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement messages, and several instances can appear in one message. It has an alignment requirement of 8n+2. Its fields are Type (55), Length (octets, excluding Type and Length), the V flag, a Reserved field, Prefix Length (the number of leftmost bits covering the network part) and the prefix itself.

When V is 1 the prefix is IPv4; when it is 0 the prefix is IPv6. Reserved MUST be initialized to 0 by the sender and MUST be ignored by the receiver. The prefix field holds a 4-byte IPv4 or a 16-byte IPv6 prefix.

Two new status codes for the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement are defined: NOT_AUTHORIZED_FOR_DELEGATED_MNP (177) and REQUESTED_DMNP_IN_USE (178).
sections.eli5: It is a small labeled note stuck onto the messages. The label says whether the block is the old kind of address or the new kind, how big the block is, and what it is.

sections.title: How the MAG and LMA Behave
sections.content:
If the mobile router's policy profile authorizes delegated prefix support, the MAG MUST include one or more DMNP options in the Proxy Binding Update. To have the LMA pick prefixes, it sends exactly one ALL_ZERO option with V=0 for IPv6, and exactly one ALL_ZERO option with V=1 for IPv4. To supply prefixes itself, it sends exactly one option with a NON_ZERO value per prefix.

On the LMA side, a Proxy Binding Update with no DMNP option means no delegated prefix support for that session. If the LMA is not configured for the feature it ignores the option. Otherwise it MUST answer with the DMNP option(s) in the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement. If a requested prefix is assigned to another node or is outside an authorized pool, the LMA MUST reject the update with REQUESTED_DMNP_IN_USE. On acceptance it MUST send status 0 with one option per allocated prefix, updates its Binding Cache entry and adds a route over the tunnel for each prefix.

On the MAG, a NOT_AUTHORIZED_FOR_DELEGATED_MNP answer means the MAG MUST NOT enable mobility for any of the mobile network prefixes. A REQUESTED_DMNP_IN_USE answer means it MUST NOT enable mobility for the requested prefixes, but it MAY retry and ask the LMA to assign. On success it records the prefixes in its Binding Update List entry and sets up a policy-based route through the tunnel. A de-registration with lifetime 0 removes this state.

On handover, if the new MAG supports the feature and already knows the prefixes, it sends them to the LMA, which authorizes them from the Binding Cache entry, the user profile or a check that they are unallocated. If the MAG does not know them, it sends 0.0.0.0 or :: and the LMA supplies them. If the new MAG does not support the feature, the previous prefixes are no longer forwarded. The RFC assumes all MAGs in a domain support the same prefix delegation mechanism.
sections.eli5: The first stop asks the home base either "please pick a block for me" or "please save this block I already have". The home base says yes or no, and both sides remember the answer so mail can find the block.

sections.title: Packet Forwarding
sections.content:
For traffic from the mobile router, the MAG MUST check that a binding exists and that the packet's source address is within a prefix delegated to that router. If the source is not part of a DMNP, the MAG MUST NOT tunnel the packet to the LMA. Packets arriving from the tunnel are decapsulated and forwarded using the inner destination address.

The LMA MUST advertise a connected route into the routing infrastructure for the prefixes delegated to all the mobile routers it serves, so it can intercept packets sent to those mobile networks. Packets whose destination matches a DMNP MUST be sent through the tunnel to the MAG where the router is attached. Packets coming up the tunnel are decapsulated, and the LMA MUST check the binding and that the source address is in a prefix delegated to a router reachable over that tunnel.

None of this applies to traffic to or from the mobile router's own home address, which still follows RFC 5213 and RFC 5844.
sections.eli5: Both ends act like doormen. They only let mail through if the return address belongs to a block that this router really owns, and the home base shouts out that it is the place to send mail for that block.

sections.title: Security and IPsec Protection
sections.content:
The DMNP option is carried like any other mobility option, so it inherits the security guidelines of RFC 5213 and needs nothing extra. DHCPv6 use follows RFC 3315 and RFC 3633, whose security considerations apply here too.

The use of DHCPv6 in this design requires message integrity protection and source authentication. The IPsec mechanism PMIPv6 already uses between MAG and LMA can protect the DHCP signaling between them as well, and the same security association used for the Proxy Binding messages also needs to protect the DHCPv6 signaling. The RFC gives example Security Policy Database and Security Association Database entries (ESP in transport mode, UDP with the DHCP port) and says they are only examples.
sections.eli5: The same locked mail pouch that protects the home base's messages should also protect the address-handout messages, so nobody can sneak in a fake one.
